I'd like to share Solidity's perspective.

tl;dr: We still think that EOF in some form is essential, because rejecting it completely will effectively kill any realistic avenue for anything but cosmetic improvements to the EVM. Sticking to the decision that was already made is the most efficient and least disruptive way to deliver it. We think that devex concerns are overstated, but we also recognize that it is perfectly rational for developers to be more concerned about short-term downsides that affect them directly than the long-term benefits for the whole platform and their sentiment does matter for adoption. We would support descoping the feature to one of the introspecting variants to address that.

---

### Reopening the debate yet again is an unnecessary distraction for the core devs and disrupts the ACD process

We know that not everyone was happy with the decision, but the technical arguments were strong enough to convince core devs on multiple occassions that EOF has merit. What seems to have changed since the last call is mainly the sentiment, not technical rationale. The issues we're talking about should be put in the right perspective. They may require some fine tuning to address specific pain points, but not total reworking of everything. The bar for rejection at this late stage should be much higher.

The best version of EOF from our perspective is one that finally ships and does not take away any more attention from planned CL changes. I.e. the version that has been already decided on and has been running on devnets. Tinkering with it can provide only marginal gains while also risking delays. It's also the version that's the easiest to adjust in future forks with small targeted EIPs. Relaxing introspection is simpler than introducing it and would not even require a new version of the container.

We firmly stand by our opinion that EOF is indispensable, because, to be honest, at this point we have absolutely zero confidence that there will ever be a viable alternative. If, after all this time, even a high-quality proposal like EOF gets dropped, we do not expect *any* meaningful EVM improvements to come to the mainnet. There is no credible counterproposal. While the debate is going on, we are seeing quickly put together proposals like [EIP-7912](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/9501) or [EIP-7921](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7921) without the same maturity and depth of research behind them and rehashing of older, long rejected EIPs. We've already been there. Once the pressure drops those are likely to share the fate of other proposals made over the years.

The main point of EOF for us is not this or that small feature - those are sorely needed, but with EOF they will come sooner or later anyway - but finally removing a blocker that has stalled the ability to add incremental improvements to the EVM. The complexity argument is ironic given that EOF used to be a much simpler proposal, meant to be delivered over two forks to reduce the scope of each, and in the end grew because one bigger upgrade was deemed more palatable. The message was that more is expected of it, not less, including [the push for of banning introspection, which came from Vitalik](https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/eof-proposal-ban-code-introspection-of-eof-accounts/12113). In our opinion, even a very minimal and stripped down EOF would have been fine as the first step. However, there's no going back to that world now. With how things are looking, it seems that there may not be much space left for EL changes in future forks, so the choice that's before us seems to be either EOF in the current form, now or nothing at all, ever.

### Developer experience issues are overstated

We think that concerns raised by tooling and applications are real, but we also feel they're a little exaggerated and are not taking the whole picture into account. The bottom line is that there is exactly zero things that they *have to* change once EOF ships. As much as we're hoping for a rapid transition, legacy EVM is not going away and is an escape hatch open for anyone who is not ready for EOF.

For the projects that do decide to switch to EOF immediately, the situation is not nearly as dire as it is made to be. The Ipsilon team has done the work of trying to convert several high-profile projects and [compiled its findings in a report](https://notes.ethereum.org/@ipsilon/eof_solc_libs_impact). To summarize it, in projects like Uniswap or OpenZeppelin, there's barely a handful of code lines that need adjustment and those are exclusively in places where low-level assembly code is used. Foundry's standard library may require some new cheats. Some of the changes can be made easier with the compiler features. It's only the projects that decided to heavily rely on assembly to optimize for gas that may need anything close to a rewrite, but they are [well aware of that and planning for the transition](https://github.com/Vectorized/solady/issues/1142).

One thing has to be pointed out: the feedback from apps and tooling did come quite late in EOF's development cycle. It started flooding in only when the experimental EOF support was released in the Solidity compiler, and this happened only very recently (in March) due to our reluctance to commit to EOF. It has an opportunity cost for us as well. We've been burned before by spending time on it only for it to be dropped from subsequent forks. The fact that recently it seems to constantly be on the verge of being dropped shows that it was not unwarranted. The fact that it is possible for features to be dropped even very late in the process is not a bad thing per se, but it does come with consequences and requires moderation. What has been happening with EOF lately feels like an abuse of that process. The mood swings are extreme.

What this has directly led to is that the compiler and layers above are delayed with respect to the EIPs and EVM implementations. We're still on track with getting it all ready for Fusaka, despite the late start, but the expectations that it should all be ready by now on all layers are unrealistic. What matters is that the lower layers are solid, well tested and ready to be released. The rest will follow. This is not unique to EOF, it's just an artifact of this extremely precarious process we have and one does not have to look far for examples. EIP-7702 due to ship in Pectra seems to be getting very similar pushback from the app layer that is suddenly waking up to the assumptions it breaks.

### We're in favor of descoping if tooling and apps strongly feel that users expect zero friction

Looking at the few changes required to convert existing projects to EOF, the main friction point seems to be the ban on gas and code introspection. Without them we'd have almost perfect source-level compatibility. And this is something we can still aim for if desired, even though it's a new requirement.

The ban has always been considered an ambitious goal. Maybe too ambitious, but as we've seen with the recent RISC-V debate, there is an understandable tendency to favor the long-term view. Not letting contracts depend on low-level implementation details makes them simpler to analyze and transform. The lack of gas observability makes them more resilient against repricing. It improves the general properties of the platform. As [EIP-7069](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7069#removing-gas-selectability) states it:

> Removing gas selectability also introduces a valuable property that future revisions to the gas schedule will benefit from: you can always overcome Out of Gas (OOG) errors by sending more gas as part of the transaction (subject to the block gas limit).

Unfortunately, what may be seen as a good thing from the broad platform perspective is also something that binds hands of app developers in a new way. EVM has many limitations that developers had to live with and some of them are defended and seen as good things today. Even something as clearly artificial as the 16-slot stack limit has been defended on the grounds of improving some imaginary interpreter properties. One can also argue that imposing certain limits and discipline pushes developers for better design. This has been often said about depending on exact gas values and yet such patterns are common. We think that in many cases these are unnecessary and can be replaced with something better. In others, relative gas limits using a mechanism like [`CALL_GAS_SPLIT`](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/9558) would be enough. In the end this is something that may require some limited fine tuning in future forks and is not something that should necessarily require scrapping the whole introspection ban.

A fully transparent transition not requiring any adjustment from userspace has never been a goal of EOF. It is a nice incidental property to have, but it also conflicts with the ability to correct some classes of past mistakes and the introduction of a new format is an opportunity to do just that. It is a non-issue if the benefits are clear and developers are motivated for the transition. Unfortunately, this recent round of negative sentiment shows that this readiness may have been overestimated. It seems that the community expectation is no friction at all. With that in mind, the demand to descope the feature to enable introspection as proposed by @frangio or @gakonst seems reasonable. We'd support them in that.

EOF is modular for a reason and can accommodate that. Even if we include introspection now, we can still leave the possibility of a future ban open for EOFv2, as long as we're careful not to let it spill into the legacy EVM. We have to keep EOF contract creation limited to EOF. Allowing this via `CREATE`/`CREATE2` on the legacy EVM would permanently lock us into code introspection, because EOF versioning does not affect those.

My position is still basically the same one that I voiced in March: https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/1374#issuecomment-2755988812

We should go with introspecting EOF, at least for the gas. Code introspection can be removed. It's still a significant upgrade in other aspects, and I still feel that these upgrades are worth it for the sake of evolving the EVM.

Lido Research team’s Soft Opposition to EOF including in Fusaka


Authors: fiddy, Vasily


EOF does not significantly impact Lido’s protocol development. On secondary effects, a rough consensus of Lido contributors is soft opposition to inclusion. All four Fusaka options risks significant post-deployment disruptions while delivering benefits that (most important of which) could be achieved either via smaller and less-disruptive EIPs (e.g. EIP-7912, the standalone version of EOF-dependent EIP-663, could solve significant pain-points on the current EVM level), or via prioritising changes outside the EVM-scope.

Core issue | Impact across all options (A – D) | Risks/Costs -- | -- | -- Smart Contract maintenance risks/costs | Every option puts pressure on multi-chain protocols to dual-maintain deployments and pipelines. New features (e.g. PAY) are either locked to EOF or, if removed, delayed indefinitely. | SC version fragmentation across chains increases operational risk and cost. Audit burden for Tooling and Infra | EOF mandates container-parsing changes in popular libraries (e.g. Solady, Snekmate, OpenZeppelin), compilers, etc. This triggers broad re-audit cycles for popular libraries that underpin DeFi. | Immediate disruption outweighs the marginal UX benefits. New and under-development code needs a re-audit cycle under EOF. Low Payoff for High Post-Deployment Costs | Due to the disruptive nature of EOF, developer time diverted to post-EOF DevRel efforts eats into potentially more impactful improvements that also need devrel efforts such as EIP-7702. | Ignoring alternative low-disruptive EIPs that can bring significant UX improvements for highly disruptive EIPs that offer marginal improvements is a cost. Uncertain roadmap longevity | Core devs continue to discuss post-EOF VM evolution. Lock-in to a transitional format today risks another format migration within a few years. | Disrupts long-term stability of (for e.g.) validator client code.

Suggested alternative: refocus engineering effort

  1. Targeted, backwards-compatible improvements (gas-cost fixes, safe-transfer opcodes available to all contracts) with measurable impact.

  2. Introduce ecosystem-disruptive changes that have significantly more upside; e.g. replacing EVM with RISC-V is disruptive with the upside that it allows us to reuse tons of mature developer tooling; otherwise, prioritise iterative non-disruptive improvements with measurable payoff.

  3. Prioritise solving compiler-level issues in the compiler-level (e.g. via using VenomIR as Solidity’s backend) instead of advocating for highly-disruptive VM-level changes.

Hi @cameel, your post is fantastic, thanks for writing this down! I have personally found it very hard to form a solid opinion on EOF, and realized after reading your post that the "mood swings" in the community are one of the reasons why I found forming an opinion so hard. These emotional swings should not influence technical processes and discussions, but they clearly do.

Your post made me realize that the community (which includes myself) seems to be aiming for a "perfect EOF" (or: "zero friction"). This is not possible, and it is certainly impossible without a feedback loop (implement a version, let developers use it, gather feedback and then improve. This can only be done on a live network with value, not on a testnet, to "battle test" it). We should accept that EOFv1 will have shortcomings. 

Current EOF bans code and gas introspection. If code/gas introspection is strongly wanted from the community, we could indeed shift the EOF scope to allow it. I am however more in favor of the version which runs on the devnets now (no code and gas introspection). We can add it later if wanted, but we cannot remove it. And developers who really need it could still use legacy EVM to do so.

EOF is, as you state in your post, also the foundation for future updates of the EVM. It has also been worked on for so long, so rejecting it now will indeed signal that big EVM improvements will never come, because even years of research dedicated to it, is apparently still not enough. Therefore we should ship it.

I will also start to contribute more to EOF consensus testing and verification.

Thanks for the post and the insights! 😄 👍

re cameel and jochem's comments, some quick comments before the call:

> Looking at the few changes required to convert existing projects to EOF, the main friction point seems to be the ban on gas and code introspection. Without them we'd have almost perfect source-level compatibility. And this is something we can still aim for if desired, even though it's a new requirement.

> Your post made me realize that the community (which includes myself) seems to be aiming for a "perfect EOF" (or: "zero friction"). This is not possible, and it is certainly impossible without a feedback loop (implement a version, let developers use it, gather feedback and then improve. This can only be done on a live network with value, not on a testnet, to "battle test" it). We should accept that EOFv1 will have shortcomings.
>
> Current EOF bans code and gas introspection. If code/gas introspection is strongly wanted from the community, we could indeed shift the EOF scope to allow it. I am however more in favor of the version which runs on the devnets now (no code and gas introspection). We can add it later if wanted, but we cannot remove it. And developers who really need it could still use legacy EVM to do so.

My perspective on this is that breaking backwards compatibility should in general **not** be part of the design goal for VM upgrades. The EVM has a network effect, and shipping large breaking changes is harmful to that effect. The EVM has broken backwards compatibility in the past -- `selfdestruct` -- but in that case it was a very selective change, had years of near-unanimous support (as far as I understand), and was motivated on its own merits.

Further, banning gas and code introspection were part of the full "EOF package" that was sold to ACD, and was one of the primary arguments for it. Without the ban, I think the new specific package of EOF should be re-justified, as variants without introspection bans were rejected in the past due to the benefit not being justified by the tradeoffs. Reducing the scope of EOF isn't completely modular or free -- there are interactions between different parts of the design, that I don't think will be fully reasoned through in a weekend.

> In others, relative gas limits using a mechanism like https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/9558 would be enough.

`CALL_GAS_SPLIT` is the same as enabling gas introspection, due to the existence of gas oracles.

> With how things are looking, it seems that there may not be much space left for EL changes in future forks, so the choice that's before us seems to be either EOF in the current form, now or nothing at all, ever.

I think this is one reason that the "urgency" feeling on EOF has been so high. There is a "now or we will never be able to improve the EVM" feeling, and I think the EL should remove this signaling -- there should be room to improve the EVM in the future, and it does not need to all be stuffed in one package.

> If, after all this time, even a high-quality proposal like EOF gets dropped, we do not expect any meaningful EVM improvements to come to the mainnet.

> EOF is, as you state in your post, also the foundation for future updates of the EVM. It has also been worked on for so long, so rejecting it now will indeed signal that big EVM improvements will never come, because even years of research dedicated to it, is apparently still not enough.

The fact that there is so much disagreement over EOF signals that its inclusion is not, in fact, a clear win. I don't think that EOF being dropped from Fusaka signals there will never be meaningful EVM improvements, but it signals that maybe they need to come in a different form. I am still in favor of smaller, incremental upgrades which each have standalone justifications.

We have some inconsistencies using minimal presets and execution requests. Would be great to have a chance to discuss this during the call, if time allows it. 
https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/4291

> but finally removing a blocker that has stalled the ability to add incremental improvements to the EVM

In the past few years core devs have accepted EIP-1153 and EIP-7702, which I think are substantial changes relating to the EVM. Part of the reason no other changes have been accepted is because many of them have been bundled into EOF and not proposed as separate solutions. Saying EVM improvements has stalled is simply not correct. There is strong desire to improve the EVM, only disagreement on whether we should retain backwards compatibility or make substantial breaking changes.

EOF is controversial, to say the least. I think it's time to take a step back and revisit incremental improvements.

> There is strong desire to improve the EVM, only disagreement on whether we should retain backwards compatibility or make substantial breaking changes.

The issue is, nearly every meaningful change runs into something breaking now. EOF *is* the way to enable incremental improvement.
Interop Testing X/Twitter Stream: https://x.com/i/broadcasts/1nAKEgkDVveJL

As a protocol developer (currently Ekubo Protocol and ex-Uniswap protocol engineer lead), my opinion has not changed since [Feb 2024](https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/pectra-network-upgrade-meta-thread/16809/55?u=moodysalem) and I am still strongly opposed to EOF.

> EOF is the way to enable incremental improvement.

It's sometimes ok to break things (that almost no one depends on), e.g. for addition of useful opcodes like TSTORE/TLOAD, which is now used ubiquitously. So I don't understand your statement that EOF is the only way to enable incremental improvement since we have made improvements in the past.

## Nethermind Team's Opinion on EOF

## Context

EOF (Ethereum Object Format) modernizes EVM bytecode by clearly separating code and data, enforcing sectioned code, and validating jumps upfront. Crucially:

- **EOF is not breaking**: Legacy contracts remain unaffected.
- **EOF is opt-in**: Existing deployment patterns don't have to change immediately.
- **EOF can call Legacy**: Escape hatches can be added
- **Legacy can call EOF**: Gas limiting dispatch patterns can still be constructed

## Technical Benefits of EOF

- **Code Sectioning**: Clearly separates code, data, and functions. This is essential for modern compilation, verification, and optimization techniques. Mixing code/data is obsolete - last common in mainstream computing over 40 years ago.
- **Eliminates dynamic jumps**: Enables static analysis and formal verification, significantly enhancing security and auditability.
- **Easier Verification**: Formal verification teams strongly prefer EOF due to its structured format, especially beneficial if we scale code size (e.g., to 256KB).  https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/1462#issuecomment-2827756221

## Sunk Cost Argument is Misplaced

- The "sunk cost" claim misunderstands EOF's status. The remaining work is minimal; extensive devnet tests and implementation are nearly complete.
- EOF has been explicitly confirmed three times in ACDE. Dropping it now undermines core dev decision-making credibility and trust.
- Ethereum's roadmap reliability matters: Repeatedly approved features shouldn't be discarded without a strong technical reason.

## "Upstream Not Ready" is a Poor Argument

- EOF’s inclusion is still ~6 months away (Fusaka), giving ample time for tooling.
- Solidity (Solady) and OpenZeppelin have already proactively prepared for EOF adoption. (Solady https://x.com/optimizoor/status/1916615756185575879,  OZ https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/compare/master...ipsilon:openzeppelin-contracts:eof)
- EIP-7702, part of the imminent Pectra fork, wouldn't have shipped if we required wallet readiness 6 months in advance.
- If Ethereum waited for complete upstream readiness before deciding protocol features, we'd never ship anything substantial.

## Current Yul Assembly Issues Are Minor and Fixable

- **`gas()` opcode**: Primarily used in `staticcall(gas(), ...)` patterns, which EOF simplifies by default (full gas forwarding). Trivial compiler pattern rewrite.
- **`extcodesize()` usage**: Mostly for contract checks; these would benefit from migrating to `extcodehash()` anyway; after propose code size increases and metering. EOF-compatible changes are straightforward.
- On-chain contract creation adjustments (create/create2) under EOF are already well-documented and accepted.

## Alternative Proposals (EIP-7912, EIP-7907) Are Not Viable for Fusaka

- **EIP-7912**: Proposes more complexity (20 new opcodes, expensive runtime lookbacks). Too new and complex for immediate inclusion.
- **EIP-7907**: Additional complexity and state burden (second indexing for code length) affecting statelessness and zk designs. Also not ready.
- Both proposals fail to match EOF’s holistic benefits and structured code improvements.
- Also adding opcodes to the legacy Evm does cause splintering at the L2 level; like `PUSH0` where contracts can be deployed but fail at runtime, whereas EOF if not supported will fail to deploy at 0 gas cost.

## Preempting Common Objections

- **"EOF is too complicated"**: EOF simplifies tooling and verification significantly long-term. Initial complexity is minimal compared to the Merge or EIP-1559.
- **"Gas issues can be fixed without EOF"**: Yes, but EOF’s structured changes deliver deeper, broader, and lasting improvements.
- **"All tooling must be EOF-ready day one"**: Not required. Legacy code continues to run unchanged; EOF is additive and optional initially.

## Regarding returning Introspection opcodes

- Team is split here; weak for adding back on pragmatic reasons, strong against for original reasons. Will voice on call.

## Conclusion: EOF Should Stay

EOF is a carefully designed, extensively tested, and already approved upgrade. Removing EOF now does not simplify Fusaka; it just creates complexity (new consensus risks, testing overhead, and trust erosion). Let’s maintain technical rigor, community trust, and roadmap reliability.

**EOF is ready - let's ship it.**

Meeting [notes](https://hackmd.io/@poojaranjan/InteropTestingNotes#Interop-Testing-Call-34-%E2%80%93-April-28-2025)

* PeerDAS Devnet 6 deprecated; Devnet 7 coming this week.
* Consensus spec update PR ([#4291](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/4291)) proposed to align EL and CL minimal specs.
* EOF Discussion: After strong debate, **EOF removed from Fusaka upgrade**.
* Option D explored (limited introspection), but community support was split.
* Focus shifted back to PeerDAS + scaling improvements for Fusaka.
* App dev feedback emphasized — stronger app-dev engagement required for future EVM upgrades.
* Future EOF considerations deferred to Glamsterdam cycle.
